obligations: createEvent must take the credentialId argument that CalendarManager passes (`calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)`, matching the Calendar interface `createEvent(event, credentialId)`) and pick the destinationCalendar entry whose credentialId equals it.
The URL must use that matched entry's externalId (`/me/calendars/<externalId>/events`).
If no entry matches, or destinationCalendar is null or empty, the request must go to the default `/me/calendar/events`. It must not fall back to another host's calendar ID.
Single-host bookings, where the only destination belongs to the calling credential, must still post to that destination calendar.
items.notes: Google's CalendarService.createEvent already does this: `destinationCalendar?.find(cal => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId || "primary"`. Office365 should mirror it. A fix that only changes the cited lines also has to add credentialId to the method signature on line 72, either as required or optional; both are fine. Falling back to the first element when nothing matches is wrong, because that reproduces the bug. The fallback has to be the default calendar.

items.defectStatement: In `checkIfIsAvailable`, line 114 compares two freshly built Dayjs objects with `===`. That checks object identity, so it is always false. As a result, the full-day "unavailable" override check (override start equals end) never fires. Without it, a slot that starts exactly at the override's start/end instant (e.g. 00:00 in the organizer's timezone) passes the remaining checks and is wrongly reported as available.
obligations: The check must compare the two adjusted times by their time value, not by object identity. Any value comparison works: `.isSame(...)`, `.valueOf()`, or comparing ISO strings.
When the override's start equals its end (after the same utcOffset adjustment), the find callback must return true, so the slot is treated as unavailable on that override day.
Overrides whose start and end differ must behave exactly as before: the other two checks (slot ends at or before start, slot starts after end) stay unchanged.
items.notes: The finding is correct. Comparing the raw `date.start` and `date.end` times without the offset is also valid, because the same offset is added to both. Comparing formatted strings at minute or millisecond precision is acceptable. Comparing only the "YYYY MM DD" day string is wrong, because it would block normal same-day overrides. A fix that still uses `==` or `===` on Dayjs objects is wrong.

items.defectStatement: In checkIfIsAvailable (slots.ts:133-135), when the slot's day has a date override and the slot falls inside it, the function returns true right away. That skips the `busy.every(...)` overlap check, so a host with an existing booking or calendar event inside the override window still shows as available and can be double-booked.
obligations: When a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot is inside the override window, the result must still depend on the busy-time overlap check. A slot that overlaps any entry in `busy` must return false.

When a date override exists for the slot's day, the working-hours check must still be skipped (the override replaces working hours for that day). A slot inside the override but outside regular working hours must not be rejected because of workingHours.

Keep existing behavior: slots outside the override window still return false. Days with no override still go through the working-hours check and then the busy check. The early return of true for an existing seated booking (currentSeats) stays as it is.
items.notes: Valid fixes include: wrapping the working-hours block in `if (!dateOverrideExist)`, or replacing the early return with a jump to the busy check (for example, a shared helper that returns the result of `busy.every`). A fix that simply deletes lines 133-135 is wrong: on override days, slots outside regular working hours would then be rejected even though the override allows them. The fix may need to change more than the cited three lines, which is acceptable. Other bugs nearby (the `===` comparison between Dayjs objects, start/end both being computed from slotStartTime in the working-hours check) are separate issues and do not need to be fixed here.

items.defectStatement: In checkIfIsAvailable, the `dateOverrides.find` callback returns true (slot rejected) as soon as any override on the slot's day doesn't contain the slot. When a day has several override ranges (e.g. 09:00–11:00 and 14:00–16:00), a slot at 10:00 that fits inside the first range is still rejected because it falls outside the second. A slot should be available if any same-day override contains it, not only if every one does. Separately, the empty-override check on line 114 compares two dayjs objects with `===`, which compares object references, so it is always false and never fires.
obligations: A slot on a day with several overrides must be accepted by the override check if at least one of that day's overrides contains it. It must be rejected only when no same-day override contains it.

If no override matches the slot's day, behavior must stay the same: `dateOverrideExist` stays false and the code goes on to the working-hours and busy checks. If any override matches the day and contains the slot, the function must still return true right away (the existing `dateOverrideExist` short-circuit).

Keep the existing timezone/utcOffset adjustment and the existing boundary rules for each override: a slot ending at or before the override start is outside, and a slot starting after the override end is outside.
An override whose start equals its end (an unavailable day) must still mark the day as having an override, and must not count as containing the slot.
items.notes: Several fixes are valid. One is to filter the overrides down to those on the slot's day, then check `some` override contains the slot. Another is a single pass that records whether the day matched and whether any override contained the slot. Whatever the approach, the result must not depend on which override `find` happens to hit first. The `===` on line 114 is a secondary bug. A fix that uses isSame or compares values is better, but a fix should not be marked wrong just for leaving the start==end case to the existing boundary checks: with start==end, every slot is either entirely before that point or after it, apart from slots that span it. Changing how partial overlap at the override end is handled (a slot that starts before the end but finishes after it) is out of scope and should not be required.

items.defectStatement: In checkIfIsAvailable (slots.ts 138-151), a slot is rejected as soon as any working-hours entry that covers its weekday fails to contain it. With several ranges on one day (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00), every slot falls outside at least one of them, so the whole day shows as unavailable. On top of that, `end` is calculated from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime, so a slot that runs past the end of a range is never caught.
obligations: Reject the slot only when no working-hours entry that covers the slot's (UTC) weekday contains it. A slot that fits inside any one range on that day must pass this check, even if it lies outside the day's other ranges.
Keep rejecting slots that fall outside every applicable range, e.g. 12:30 on a 09-12/13-17 day, or any time before or after all of the day's ranges.

Keep the current behaviour when workingHours is empty or when no entry covers the slot's weekday: the check must not reject the slot, and it goes on to the busy check. Keep using UTC minutes (hour*60+minute), matching how WorkingHours startTime/endTime are stored.
items.notes: The finding is correct. Computing `end` from slotStartTime is a second bug in the same lines. A fix should compare the slot's end (slotEndTime) against the range end, but this is not required for the main issue, so don't fail a fix that only corrects the find-vs-some logic. If a fix does use slotEndTime, watch slots that cross UTC midnight: hour*60+minute wraps to a small number there. Several fixes are valid: `!some(...)`, a filter over the applicable ranges followed by a containment check, and similar. Important: a naive `!workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(day) && contains)` rejects slots on days that no entry covers, where the original code let them pass. Accept that only if the grader judges it intended. Ideally the fix applies the containment check only when at least one entry covers that day, so empty or non-covering workingHours still behave as before.

items.defectStatement: In checkIfIsAvailable (slots.ts 138-151), `end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, the same value as `start`, so the end of the slot is never checked against `workingHour.endTime`. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past them is accepted. The check is also inverted: `find` returns a truthy entry for any working-hours entry on that weekday that does not contain the slot. When a day has several disjoint entries (e.g. 9-12 and 13-17, or the split entries getWorkingHours produces around midnight), every slot fails at least one entry, so every slot is rejected.
obligations: The end bound must use the slot's real end (slot start + eventLength, i.e. slotEndTime). A slot that starts inside a working-hours window but ends after its endTime must be reported unavailable.

When the slot's weekday has several working-hours entries, the slot must be accepted if at least one entry fully contains it (start >= startTime and end <= endTime). It must not be rejected just because some other entry on the same day fails to contain it.

Keep the existing behavior around this check: an empty workingHours array (the default) must not reject slots, the date-override path above still takes precedence, and accepted slots still go through the busy-time check.
Keep the comparison in UTC minutes-of-day against the UTC weekday, matching how getWorkingHours encodes entries.
items.notes:
Valid fixes include `some` with containment and negation, or `every` with a non-containment test. Either works if a slot passes when any entry on its day contains it.

Trap: getWorkingHours clamps endTime to MINUTES_DAY_END = 1439, so a window ending at midnight is stored with endTime 1439. If the end is computed as startMinutes + eventLength, a slot ending exactly at midnight gives 1440. If it is computed as slotEndTime.hour()*60+minute, it wraps to 0. Neither should be a reason to fail a fix that otherwise handles the general case, but a fix that newly rejects normal in-hours slots is wrong. Don't require handling of slots that span midnight across two entries.

Judgment call: when the weekday has no working-hours entry at all, the current code accepts the slot. A fix that rejects it ("no entry contains the slot") or one that only applies the check when the day has entries are both acceptable, since slots are generated from working hours anyway. The finding's diagnosis is accurate.

items.defectStatement: In checkIfIsAvailable's date-override branch (slots.ts 117-124), a slot counts as outside the override only when it ends at or before the override start, or starts strictly after the override end. So slots that partly overlap the override are wrongly offered as available. With a 10:00–11:00 override, 09:30–10:30, 10:30–11:30 and a slot starting exactly at 11:00 all pass.
obligations: The callback must return true (slot not available) whenever the slot start is before the override start or the slot end is after the override end. Both are compared against the same offset-adjusted values: dayjs(date.start/date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').
A slot that fits fully inside the override must still be accepted, including at the boundaries: start == override start, or end == override end (e.g. 10:00–11:00 inside a 10:00–11:00 override).
Slots starting at or after the override end (e.g. 11:00 for an override ending at 11:00) and slots ending at or before the override start must still be rejected.
Keep the existing utcOffset adjustment and the same-day matching. Do not change which day an override applies to.
items.notes: Any equivalent comparison is fine, e.g. `slotStartTime.isBefore(start) || slotEndTime.isAfter(end)`, or the negation of isBetween with inclusive bounds. Line 114 compares dayjs objects with ===, so it is always false. That is a separate issue and not required here. Because of the `.find` structure, a day with several overrides rejects a slot that fits one override but falls outside another. This is outside the cited lines, so a fix limited to the bounds condition is acceptable. Graders should not require it, but may credit a fix that mentions it.

items.defectStatement: In getSlots (packages/lib/slots.ts 216-224), each override's start/end is shifted by the organizer→invitee offset and then turned into minutes with `hour()*60+minute()`, which keeps only the time of day. When the shift crosses midnight the day change is thrown away. Ranges that cross completely (e.g. 20:00-23:00 at +6h → 02:00-05:00) are still attached to the original startOfInviteeDay, so slots appear on the wrong day. Ranges that cross partway (e.g. 20:00-23:00 at +3h → 23:00-02:00) end up with endTime < startTime and are silently skipped by buildSlots (`start >= end` → continue), so the override's slots disappear. Negative offsets have the same problem (01:00-03:00 at -6h shows as 19:00-21:00 on the same day).
obligations: startTime/endTime must keep the day change after the timezone shift: they are minutes relative to the start of the invitee's day and may go below 0 or above 1440, or must be clipped/split correctly. They must not wrap modulo 24h.

A shifted override that ends after midnight must not end up with endTime < startTime, and must not be silently dropped. At least the part that falls inside the invitee day must still produce slots at the right times.
Overrides that do not cross midnight after the shift, including offset 0 (same timezone), must give exactly the same startTime/endTime as now.
Keep the existing userIds mapping and the offset calculation from organizer and invitee utcOffset.
items.notes: Trap: override.start/end are not real instants. getUserAvailability builds them as the organizer's wall-clock time stored as a UTC Date (`dayjs.utc(date).hour(h).minute(m)`). The finding's suggested `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).diff(startOfInviteeDay)` would therefore apply the timezone conversion a second time, so it is not automatically correct. A valid fix computes the shifted UTC-wall-clock value (`dayjs.utc(start).add(offset,'minute')`) and takes its minute difference from the UTC midnight of the override's/invitee's calendar date. Accept any equivalent approach, for example clamping to [0, 1440] or allowing values outside that range, as long as the day change is kept. Fully fixing this would also mean the activeOverrides filter (line 207, outside the cited lines) picks up overrides from neighbouring organizer days that land on this invitee day. A fix limited to the cited lines that only clamps or keeps the day change is acceptable; don't require the filter change. Note that buildSlots only produces slots inside the day, so leaving negative or >1440 values unclamped is harmless.

items.defectStatement: In scheduleEmailReminders.ts lines 53-77, one try/catch wraps the whole cancellation loop. If a single `client.request` to SendGrid's scheduled_sends cancel endpoint throws (for example a 4xx for a batch that was already cancelled or sent), the loop stops: the remaining cancelled-booking reminders are never cancelled at SendGrid, so those emails still go out. The deletes already collected are also never run, because Prisma delete calls are lazy and only execute when awaited, and the `Promise.all` is skipped.
obligations: A SendGrid cancel failure for one reminder must not stop the others: every remaining reminder in remindersToCancel still gets its cancel request.
Every reminder whose SendGrid cancel succeeds must actually have its workflowReminder row deleted (the delete is awaited or otherwise executed), even when other reminders in the batch failed.
Errors must still be caught and logged and must not escape the handler: the code after this block (scheduling unscheduled reminders and sending the response) must still run.

Keep the existing behavior: the same request body (batch_id = referenceId, status "cancel") is sent to /v3/user/scheduled_sends, and the rows deleted are the ones selected by the remindersToCancel query.
items.notes: Several fixes are valid: a try/catch inside the loop around each request (and its delete); Promise.allSettled over per-reminder async tasks; or awaiting each delete inline. It is up to the fix whether a reminder whose SendGrid cancel failed gets deleted or kept for retry. Either is acceptable as long as the other reminders are processed. Context: the cancelled flag is only set (in emailReminderManager.ts) for reminders that have a referenceId, so null batch_ids are not the main trigger. A fix that only moves `await Promise.all` outside the try, but still lets one failure end the loop, does not fix the defect.

items.defectStatement: In deleteScheduledSMSReminder, `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` sit in the same try block. If the Twilio cancel throws, the DB delete is skipped and the error is only logged. The workflowReminder row stays behind as an orphan (scheduled=true, a referenceId, no cancelled flag), and nothing ever cleans it up or retries.
obligations: The workflowReminder row with id `reminderId` must still be removed (or reliably marked handled/cancelled) when `twilio.cancelSMS` throws. A Twilio failure must not stop the DB cleanup.
When `referenceId` is non-null, keep trying to cancel the SMS with Twilio. When `referenceId` is null, skip the Twilio call and just delete the row.

The function must keep swallowing and logging errors (both Twilio and Prisma) rather than throwing. Callers call it fire-and-forget inside forEach without awaiting, so a throw would become an unhandled rejection.
Keep the signature `(reminderId: number, referenceId: string | null)` unchanged; callers in handleCancelBooking, handleNewBooking, bookings.tsx and workflows.tsx depend on it.
items.notes: The finding overstates one point. Deleting the DB row does not stop a Twilio-scheduled SMS. If cancelSMS fails, the message may still go out whether or not the row is deleted, so a fix is not required to guarantee the SMS is never sent. The real, fixable defect is the skipped DB delete that leaves an orphan row. Any of these is a valid fix: a separate try/catch around each call, putting the delete in `finally`, or running the delete regardless with its own error handling. Marking the row cancelled for a later retry is also acceptable, but only if it is consistent with how the email manager uses `cancelled: true`. A fix that just reorders the calls (delete first, then cancel) is acceptable too, as long as a delete failure doesn't silently skip the Twilio cancel, or the trade-off is clearly reasonable.

items.defectStatement: In the catch block (lines 189-196), retryCount is written as `reminder.retryCount + 1`, using the value read at the start of the cron run. If two runs of the handler overlap, or the row changes in between, both write the same value and one retry is lost. Retries get undercounted, so the `retryCount > 1` cleanup can come later than it should.
obligations: The catch-block update must increment retryCount atomically in the database (e.g. Prisma `retryCount: { increment: 1 }`), not write a value computed from the in-memory `reminder.retryCount`.
It must still update only the row with `id: reminder.id`, and must still log the error afterwards, as now.
The code must not throw out of the loop in a new way (no added rethrow), so the other reminders keep being processed and the handler still returns 200.
items.notes: This is a narrow race. The handler is a cron job, so it only happens if runs overlap. Any atomic form is acceptable: Prisma `increment`, a raw `SET retryCount = retryCount + 1`, or a conditional update / optimistic check. The else branch at lines 179-186 has the same defect, but it is outside the cited lines, so a fix limited to 189-196 is fine. Unrelated problems should not count against the fix, e.g. the deleteMany `retryCount gt 1` clause not being limited to SMS, or the update inside the catch throwing on its own.

items.defectStatement: The `catch` block in the per-reminder loop (lines 189-197) now awaits `prisma.workflowReminder.update` to bump `retryCount`, and nothing guards that call. If it rejects (for example, the record was already deleted by a concurrent run's `deleteMany`, which now also removes rows with `retryCount > 1`, or the DB has a transient error), the exception escapes the catch. That aborts the `for` loop, so the remaining reminders are never processed and the error is never logged. The handler then fails instead of returning 200.
obligations: A rejection from the retryCount update in the catch path must not escape the handler: the loop must continue to the next reminder and the handler must still reach `res.status(200)`.
On a scheduling error, the code must still try to increment `retryCount` to `reminder.retryCount + 1` for that reminder. Do not remove the retry bookkeeping.
The original scheduling error must still be logged, even when the retryCount update fails, so that error is not lost or replaced.
items.notes: Several fixes are valid: wrap the update in its own try/catch, use `.catch()` on the promise, log before the update and then guard it, or use `updateMany` (which does not throw when no row matches) as long as transient errors are also caught. Moving only the log above the update does not solve the problem, because a throw would still abort the loop. The success-path updates inside the try block are already covered by the outer catch, so they are out of scope. Do not count it as a defect if a fix leaves them alone.

items.defectStatement: The new else branch (lines 178-186) adds 1 to retryCount whenever `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns a falsy value. But `scheduleSMS` only returns `undefined` when the user or team is locked for SMS sending (`isLockedForSMSSending`, twilioProvider.ts:90-95). Real Twilio and rate-limit failures throw and are already handled in the catch block. Because the new deleteMany removes reminders with retryCount > 1, a reminder for a locked user or team is permanently deleted after a couple of cron runs, when it should have been retried once the lock is lifted.
obligations: A falsy (undefined) return from scheduleSMS because of an SMS lock must not increase retryCount or otherwise count as a failure. The reminder must stay unscheduled and retryCount must stay the same, so a later cron run can schedule it once the lock is lifted.
The success path must still set scheduled=true and referenceId=sid.
The catch block must still increase retryCount when a real send error is thrown (Twilio error, rate limit).
items.notes: The finding is accurate: scheduleSMS returns undefined only on the lock path, and otherwise returns the Twilio response or throws. Several fixes are valid: drop the retryCount update from the else branch (empty branch, log only, or remove the branch), or check the lock explicitly and skip the increment. A fix that still increments retryCount in this branch, even conditionally on some unrelated value, does not resolve the defect. A separate issue is out of scope for this finding: the retryCount>1 clause in deleteMany has no method filter, so it can match reminders of any method.

items.defectStatement: At line 31, `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError when the body is missing, malformed, or has wrong types (for example, a non-integer userId or a missing appSlug or keys). The handler is a plain Next.js API route with no try/catch and no error-mapping wrapper such as defaultResponder, so the error goes uncaught and the client gets a 500 instead of a 400 client error.
obligations: An invalid or missing request body (bad or missing userId, appSlug or keys) must produce a 4xx response (400 expected) with a JSON message, not an uncaught exception or a 500.
A valid body must still parse to the same typed fields (userId, appSlug, keys) and continue through the existing user, app, decrypt and upsert flow unchanged.
The validation must still run after the 403 checks for credential sharing and the webhook secret, so unauthenticated requests still get 403.
items.notes: Several fixes are valid: `safeParse` with an early `return res.status(400)...`, or `parse` wrapped in a try/catch that returns 400 on ZodError. Including the Zod error details in the response is optional. The `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` call at lines 57-59 can also throw on bad keys, but it is outside the cited line and a fix does not need to handle it. The "leaking exception path" part of the finding is overstated: Next.js does not expose the stack trace in production.

items.defectStatement: In SalesforceCalendarService.getClient (lines 75-99), every client creation calls `fetch` against login.salesforce.com directly. Because it skips `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "salesforce", credential.userId)`, the CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT path is never used when credential sharing is enabled. Failure is also detected with `response.statusText !== "OK"`, so a successful response with an empty or different status text (HTTP/2 often sends none) throws a spurious 400. As written, each instantiation also costs one token request and one DB write.
obligations: The token refresh request must go through `refreshOAuthTokens(...)` with app slug "salesforce" and the credential's user id. With credential sync enabled and a userId present, the sync endpoint must be used. Otherwise it falls back to the Salesforce refresh_token POST, keeping the same grant_type, client_id, client_secret and refresh_token parameters.
Success or failure must be judged by HTTP status (`response.ok` or an equivalent status-code check), not by `statusText`. A non-OK response must still produce an error.

Keep the existing behavior: validate the response with `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and save it to the credential while keeping the original refresh_token (and instance_url if the response lacks it). Invalid token payloads must still be rejected.
items.notes: The main defects are bypassing `refreshOAuthTokens` and the `statusText` check. The finding's "refresh only when missing or expired" advice should not be required. Salesforce token responses include no expires_in (only an `issued_at` string), and jsforce already refreshes on its own when `refreshToken` is set. A fix that avoids the eager refresh in some reasonable way is fine but optional. Note that `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on failure rather than returning success:false, so the `!success` branch never runs; this is harmless. A related issue sits just outside the cited lines: line 106 passes the old `credentialKey.access_token` to jsforce rather than the refreshed token, so the eager refresh does not even help the current connection. A fix that also passes the new token is a plus but is not required for these lines.

items.defectStatement: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts) returns the whole Zod safeParse result `{ success, data }`, not the parsed object. Line 97 assigns that wrapper to `key`, and lines 98-100 save it as `credential.key`. After the first token refresh, the stored key looks like `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, so the next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` at line 75 throws and the Google Calendar credential stays broken.
obligations: The value saved as `credential.key` must be the plain credential object, with access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date, scope and token_type at the top level. It must not be the `{ success, data }` wrapper.
The saved key must include the refreshed access_token and expiry_date, and it must still validate against googleCredentialSchema when the service is created again.

Keep the refreshed-token validation that the new code added (`parseRefreshTokenResponse` or equivalent). Keep the existing update-by-`credential.id` call and the later `myGoogleAuth.setCredentials` behavior.
items.notes: Several fixes are valid: `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data`, destructuring `{ data }`, or saving `googleCredentials` after the parse succeeds. Going back to `googleCredentialSchema.parse` also stops the corruption, but it skips the credential-sync schema path, so it is weaker. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws when the parse fails, so checking `success` is optional. office365calendar (line 264) handles this correctly with `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data`. Watch out for a fix that only renames the variable and still saves the wrapper object.

items.defectStatement: On every path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` writes the literal string "refresh_token" into `data.refresh_token` whenever the parsed response doesn't include one. That includes the normal non-sharing path. Office365 parses with a schema where `refresh_token` is optional, then spreads `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credentials and saves the result (CalendarService.ts:263-272). So when Microsoft's refresh response leaves out `refresh_token`, the real stored token gets replaced by "refresh_token", and every later refresh sends that fake value and fails.
obligations: On the non-sharing path (flag off or `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` unset), the returned data must not contain a placeholder `refresh_token` when the provider response has none. Merging it into stored credentials (office365's spread) must leave the existing refresh token untouched. The key can be absent or undefined, but it cannot be a fake string.
A real `refresh_token` in the response must still come through unchanged.
The credential-sharing/sync path (`minimumTokenResponseSchema` branch) may keep the placeholder, since downstream schemas that require `refresh_token` may depend on it.
Keep the existing behaviour: throw on a failed parse and return the safeParse result object (`success`/`data`).
items.notes: Any of these is a valid fix: only inject when the sharing branch was taken, pass a flag to control it, or drop the injection entirely on the non-sharing path. Moving the `if` inside the sharing branch is enough. Zoom and Salesforce are not hurt on the non-sharing path because their schemas already require or handle `refresh_token`. Google passes in the full stored credentials, so the refresh token is already there. Office365 is the caller that actually breaks. Don't accept a fix that still overwrites the refresh token with any made-up value on the normal path.

items.defectStatement: In the uniqueGuests filter (lines 74-78), both checks compare case-sensitively. The existing-attendee check uses `guest === attendee.email`, so "Foo@x.com" is not seen as a duplicate of an existing "foo@x.com" and gets added again. The blacklist is lowercased when it is built (line 71), but it is compared against the raw guest string, which the schema does not lowercase (`z.string().email()`). Any guest email containing uppercase letters therefore never matches the blacklist and gets past the filter.
obligations: A guest that matches an existing attendee's email in any casing must be filtered out, so the attendee comparison has to be case-insensitive on both sides.
A guest that matches a blacklisted email in any casing (e.g. "BAD@X.COM" when "bad@x.com" is blacklisted) must be filtered out.
Guests that are not duplicates and not blacklisted must still go through. The existing behavior stays: an empty result throws emails_must_be_unique_valid.
items.notes: Valid fixes include lowercasing inside the comparisons, or normalizing guests and attendee emails before filtering. Either approach is fine as long as both sides of each comparison are normalized. If a fix only lowercases the guest for the blacklist check and leaves the attendee comparison case-sensitive, it is incomplete. Optional extras that are not required: trimming blacklist entries and deduplicating emails within the guests array itself.

items.defectStatement: `ZAddGuestsInputSchema.guests` is a plain `z.array(z.string().email())` and nothing checks that the emails are unique. The handler (addGuests.handler.ts:74-78) only drops guests who are already attendees or blacklisted. It never removes duplicates within the input, so a request like `["a@x.com","a@x.com"]` makes `attendees.createMany` insert two attendee rows for the same email. `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` also receives the duplicated list.
obligations: The schema must stop duplicate emails in `guests` from reaching the handler. It can either reject the input with a validation error (e.g. refine/superRefine) or dedupe it (e.g. transform). Either way, `createMany` must never see the same email twice from one request.
Each entry must still be validated with `z.string().email()`, and `bookingId: z.number()` must stay as it is.
A list of distinct valid emails must still parse unchanged, so existing clients keep working. The parsed output must still be a string[] of emails, which the handler uses with `.filter`/`.map`.
items.notes: The finding is confirmed: the handler's `uniqueGuests` filter only checks existing attendees and the blacklist, not duplicates within the request. Rejecting duplicates and silently deduping are both valid fixes. Case-insensitive comparison (e.g. lowercasing before comparing) is a bonus but not required. Note that the handler's attendee comparison is case-sensitive, so lowercasing the stored values would change behavior. Don't require the handler to change, because the fix is limited to the schema lines.

items.defectStatement: On lines 46-48 the authorization flag joins `isTeamAdmin(...)` and `isTeamOwner(...)` with `&&`, so it is true only when the user passes both checks. `isTeamAdmin` matches role ADMIN or OWNER, so in practice only team OWNERs pass. A team ADMIN who is not the organizer or an attendee gets a FORBIDDEN error when adding guests to a team booking, even though the variable name and intent say admins or owners should be allowed.
obligations: A user with an accepted ADMIN membership on the booking's event-type team (and no OWNER role) must count as authorized, so `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is truthy for them.
A user with an accepted OWNER membership on the team must still count as authorized.
Users who are neither team admin nor team owner must still be denied unless they are the organizer or an attendee. Bookings with no team (teamId falls back to 0) must not grant team-admin access.
The flag must keep working with the later `!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee` check. Truthy/falsy semantics are enough, because `isTeamAdmin` returns a membership object or false.
items.notes: The finding is correct. These fixes are all valid: replacing `&&` with `||`; calling only `isTeamAdmin`, since its query already includes role OWNER (`OR: [{role:"ADMIN"},{role:"OWNER"}]`); or coercing the result with `!!`. Short-circuiting with `||` is fine. Do not penalize a fix for keeping the `?? 0` fallback for teamId.

items.defectStatement: In addGuests.handler.ts lines 70-77, the blacklist is lowercased but each raw guest address is checked with `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`, with no lowercasing and no plus-alias stripping. So an authorized organizer, attendee or admin can add a blacklisted address just by changing its case (e.g. `Blocked@x.com`) or adding a `+tag` (e.g. `blocked+1@x.com`). handleNewBooking blocks both forms because it compares `extractBaseEmail(guest).toLowerCase()`.
obligations: A guest must be filtered out when its base email (local part before '+' plus domain) matches a BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entry, ignoring case on both sides. Example: with `blocked@x.com` blacklisted, `BLOCKED@x.com` and `blocked+foo@x.com` must both be removed.

Guests that are not blacklisted must still be kept and stored with their original address string. Normalization is only for the comparison; the value written to `uniqueGuests` / `guestsFullDetails` must not be rewritten.

Keep the existing filter that drops guests who are already attendees, and keep the BAD_REQUEST `emails_must_be_unique_valid` error when no guests remain. An unset or empty BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS must still block nothing.
items.notes: `extractBaseEmail` is in `@calcom/lib/extract-base-email` and splits on '+' and '@'. A fix can either import it or do the same normalization inline; both are fine. The fix needs that import (outside the cited lines), so accept a fix that assumes it. Optional extras that should not be required: trimming blacklist entries, and making the already-attendee check case-insensitive. Related problem outside the cited lines: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` sends to the raw `guests` list instead of `uniqueGuests`, so blacklisted addresses may still get emails. Mentioning it is fine, but a fix limited to lines 70-77 is not expected to change that call.

items.defectStatement: After a successful cache deletion, `deleteCacheMutation` (lines 42-50) only shows a toast and calls the optional parent `onSuccess`. It never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, which is where `cacheUpdatedAt` comes from. In SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper, `onSuccess` is wired to the optional `onChanged` prop, which may be undefined or may not refetch. When that happens the dropdown keeps showing the stale "cache last updated" entry and the "delete cached data" option.
obligations: After a successful deleteCache mutation, the `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query must be invalidated or refetched, with or without a parent `onSuccess` callback, so `cacheUpdatedAt` refreshes.
Keep the existing success toast (`cache_deleted_successfully`) and the call to the optional parent `onSuccess?.()` on success.
Keep the error toast (`error_deleting_cache`) on failure.
items.notes: `utils` is declared on line 52, below the cited block. A fix inside lines 42-50 must either move or redeclare `trpc.useUtils()` above the mutation, or reference `utils` only inside a callback that runs later, after the component has rendered. A reference inside a callback is valid at runtime because of closure timing. Invalidating in onSuccess or in onSettled are both fine. Also invalidating `viewer.apps.integrations` is optional and not required.

items.defectStatement: In requestReschedule (bookings.tsx 553-567), `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` throws away every promise. That includes the now-async `getCalendar(...)` plus `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting`. So the calendar and video deletions are never awaited: they run fire-and-forget, any rejection is unhandled, and the reschedule email and BOOKING_CANCELLED webhook below can go out before the external events are actually deleted.
obligations: Every deletion promise (getCalendar + deleteEvent for `_calendar` refs, deleteMeeting for `_video` refs) must be collected and awaited before the code continues to sendRequestRescheduleEmail. Examples: Promise.all or Promise.allSettled over a map, or a for...of loop with await.
No deletion rejection may be left unhandled. Either it is caught and logged per item, or it reaches the awaiting caller.

Keep the existing per-ref logic: skip refs with no uid, pass `builder.calendarEvent` and `bookingRef.externalCalendarId` to deleteEvent, look up the credential with credentialsMap.get(bookingRef.type), and treat a null calendar safely (calendar?.).
items.notes: The finding is overstated on one point: no try/catch wraps this code in requestReschedule. The real problem is unawaited promises and unhandled rejections. These fixes are all valid: Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, a sequential for...of loop, or per-item .catch with logging. Strict Promise.all makes the mutation fail if one deletion fails. Catching or settling each deletion keeps the email/webhook flow going. Both are fine as long as the promises are awaited. Do not accept a fix that only wraps the forEach in try/catch or leaves `forEach(async ...)` in place.

items.defectStatement: In packages/app-store/index.ts, every entry of the `appStore` object is a bare `import("./x")` expression. These run as soon as the object literal is evaluated, which happens when `@calcom/app-store` is first imported. So every app module and its heavy dependencies (googleapis, Office365, Stripe, etc.) still load eagerly, and the dynamic-import conversion doesn't actually make anything lazy.
obligations: Importing `@calcom/app-store` must not by itself start loading any app module. Each entry has to defer its `import()`, for example as a thunk `() => import("./x")`, so that a module loads only when its key is looked up.

All 28 existing keys must stay, with the same names and the same target paths: applecalendar through sylapsvideo, including exchange2013calendar, exchange2016calendar, exchangecalendar, facetime and sylapsvideo. Do not drop or rename any.

Looking up a key must still resolve to the app module namespace, so callers can keep reading `.lib` / `.lib.PaymentService` / `.lib.CalendarService` / `.lib.VideoApiAdapter` as before. If the entries become functions, the callers (getCalendar.ts, videoClient.ts, handlePayment.ts, deletePayment.ts, handleCancelBooking.ts, bookings.tsx) must invoke them, e.g. `await appStore[key]?.()`. Unknown or undefined keys must still give a falsy value and must not throw.
items.notes: The finding is correct. Callers currently do `await appStore[key]` on a promise, so a thunk-only change to index.ts without updating the callers would make every lookup return a function, and `.lib` would be undefined there. A candidate restricted to the cited lines should at least acknowledge or handle this. Other valid ways to defer loading: a getter or a function `getApp(key)` that runs a switch over `import()` calls, or memoized thunks. All are acceptable if loading is deferred and the module shape is preserved. Keeping bare `import()` values and only reordering keys or adding `await` does not fix the problem. Key order is irrelevant.

items.defectStatement: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs` (bleve.go:144-154) loops over `b.cache` without holding `b.cacheMu`. `BuildIndex` writes to the same map at line 138. TotalDocs is called from the Prometheus metrics collector (bleve_index_metrics.go:96) and at search init, so it can run while an index is being built. That is a Go map read/write race, which can crash with "concurrent map iteration and map write".
obligations: TotalDocs must hold b.cacheMu (`RLock` is enough; it is a `sync.RWMutex`) for the whole time it iterates b.cache, and must release it on every return path.
BuildIndex must keep taking the write lock (`Lock`) around the `b.cache[key] = idx` assignment.
Keep TotalDocs' current behavior: return the sum of `DocCount()` over all cached indexes and skip any index whose `DocCount()` returns an error.
No deadlock: TotalDocs must not take the write lock or lock again while it already holds the lock.
items.notes: The finding overstates the regression. Before this PR, TotalDocs also ran without the lock, so BuildIndex holding the lock never serialized it against TotalDocs, and the race was already there. The required fix is the same either way. Valid alternatives: copy the index list (or snapshot it) while holding RLock, then call DocCount after unlocking; or hold RLock with `defer` for the whole loop. A plain `Lock()` is acceptable but not ideal. Another accessor (line 61) already uses the RLock/RUnlock pattern, which shows the expected style.

items.defectStatement: The diff removed the whole-function `cacheMu` lock from `BuildIndex`. Now only the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write is locked, so concurrent calls for the same NamespacedResource run completely in parallel. Several paths can trigger that: `getOrCreateIndex` from Search, `handleEvent`, and the init workers. Each concurrent call opens its own bleve index (`bleve.New` on the same `<Root>/<ns>/<resource>.<group>` dir for file indexes) and repeats the full ListIterator/Write/Flush. `IndexTenants` gets incremented more than once, and the last writer replaces the earlier index in the cache. The replaced index is never closed, and any caller already holding it keeps writing to it.
obligations: Concurrent BuildIndex/getOrCreateIndex calls for the same key must not build in parallel, so the same directory is never opened twice and the same build is never repeated at once. Acceptable approaches: per-key lock, singleflight, or checking the cache again under a lock before building.
Builds for different keys must still be able to run concurrently: the init errgroup workers should not be serialized by a single global lock held across the build.

The cache map must still only be read and written under `cacheMu`, and the cache must hold exactly one index per key. When a key loses a race it must not replace the winner or double-count the `IndexTenants` metric.
Callers must get back a usable, fully flushed index, and error returns must not leave a partial index in the cache or hold any lock after returning.
items.notes: The old code had a gap too: `getOrCreateIndex` (resource/search.go:287) calls GetIndex outside any lock, so two callers could already both miss and build one after the other. Holding the global lock across the whole build only serialized those builds; it did not deduplicate them. A fix that simply puts the global lock back around the whole build stops the parallel builds, but it blocks GetIndex and all other keys while a build runs, and it still allows a second build to follow the first. Better fixes are per-key singleflight or a cache check under the lock. These may be done in BuildIndex or in getOrCreateIndex/build, but the cited lines are in BuildIndex. The finding gives the directory as Root/Namespace/Group; the actual path is Root/Namespace/"resource.group", which is a minor error. `TotalDocs` also reads the cache without taking the lock, a related problem that is out of scope here.

items.defectStatement: GrafanaRuleListItem passes only `promRule` to RuleActionsButtons (no `rule`). Without a ruler rule, AlertRuleMenu never renders the Pause/Resume item, because it checks `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` and MenuItemPauseRule needs a `RulerGrafanaRuleDTO` (it reads `grafana_alert.uid` / `is_paused`). So Grafana rules in the new list view have no Pause/Resume control, even when the Prometheus-based pause ability check passes.
obligations: Grafana rules in the new list view must show a working Pause/Resume menu item when the user is allowed to pause, and toggling it must pause or resume the right rule (by uid, within the Grafana group).
Resume vs. pause state must reflect the rule's current paused status (e.g. from promRule.isPaused or fetched ruler data).

Existing callers that pass a ruler `rule` (e.g. the rule viewer/details page) must keep their current pause, delete and duplicate behavior. The permission/ability gating (canPause) must be preserved, so users without permission still see no control.
Must not drop the other actions the list currently shows (edit, silence, export, copy link, and so on).
items.notes: Valid fixes: (a) make AlertRuleMenu/MenuItemPauseRule accept a GrafanaPromRuleDTO (uid + isPaused) as the pause source; (b) fetch the ruler rule on demand, for example a wrapper at line 47 or a hook in RuleActionsButtons that loads the ruler rule by uid and passes it as `rule`. A fix limited to line 47 is only valid if it really gets ruler data (for example a wrapper that fetches it). Passing `rule={rule}` with the prom DTO is a type error and does not fix anything. Related issue not in the finding: Delete is also hidden, because it requires `rulerRule`. Fixing it is a bonus, not required.

items.defectStatement: In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, when `rule` is undefined (callers pass skipToken for non-Grafana rules), useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable returns `loading: false`. That makes `MaybeSupported` equal AlwaysSupported, so Duplicate comes out as `toAbility(AlwaysSupported, grafana create permission)`. AlertRuleMenu ORs this Grafana ability with the ruler one when computing `canDuplicate`, so Duplicate shows up for data-source rules whenever the user can create Grafana rules, even if the ruler ability says it is not supported or not allowed.
obligations: When `rule` is undefined, the Duplicate ability must not come out as both supported and allowed. Either `supported` or `allowed` (or both) must be false, whatever permissions the user has.

When `rule` is undefined, the other mutating abilities (Update, Delete, Pause, Restore, DeletePermanently, Silence, ModifyExport) must also stay unsupported or disallowed. Today they already are, through isEditable/isRemovable being false and isAlertingRule being false.

For a defined GrafanaPromRuleDTO, behavior must not change: still NotSupported while the folder is loading, still AlwaysSupported once it has loaded, and plugin-provided rules still cannot be duplicated. Immutable rules (provisioned or plugin-provided) must still block Update, Delete, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently.
items.notes: Any of these fixes is valid: treat `!rule` like loading (`!rule || loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported`); make duplicateSupported false when there is no rule; or return early with an all-NotSupported ability map for an undefined rule. The bug can be fixed inside the cited lines; there is no need to change useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable. View and Explore are also AlwaysSupported for an undefined rule. AlertRuleMenu does not read those from the Grafana hook, so a fix may leave them as they are or set them to NotSupported. Don't require it. RuleActionsButtons.V2 only reads Update from this hook, and Update is already false for an undefined rule, so the visible bug is Duplicate in AlertRuleMenu.

items.defectStatement: In RuleActionsButtons.V2 the silence drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the new list view the component gets only `promRule` and `rule` is undefined. AlertRuleMenu can still show "Silence notifications" there, because it checks silence permission through the Grafana prom rule. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true, but nothing renders, so Silence silently does nothing for prom-only Grafana alerting rules.
obligations: When `rule` is undefined and `promRule` is a Grafana alerting rule (prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule), setting showSilenceDrawer must render a silence drawer/editor for that rule's uid (promRule.uid).
Existing behavior must be preserved: when `rule` is a Grafana ruler alerting rule, the drawer still renders using that rule's grafana_alert.uid.
No drawer may render for non-Grafana rules or for Grafana recording rules, and the drawer must still close via onClose (setShowSilenceDrawer(false)).
The code must type-check: SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer currently requires `rulerRule: RulerGrafanaRuleDTO`, so a prom rule must not be passed as `rulerRule` without adapting the props.
items.notes: SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only uses rulerRule.grafana_alert.uid (to set the SilencesEditor ruleUid and in its memo comparison). Several fixes are valid: (a) change the drawer to take a `ruleUid` prop (or accept either rule type) and update its other caller in components/rules/RuleActionsButtons.tsx; (b) render SilencesEditor with promRule.uid inline; (c) compute the uid from either rule (rule?.grafana_alert.uid ?? promRule.uid) and pass it. Building a fake RulerGrafanaRuleDTO from the prom rule is hacky; accept it only if it is type-safe and correct. A fix that changes the drawer's props beyond the cited lines must keep the other caller working.

items.defectStatement: In `CleanUpService.Run` (pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go:77), the cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. Every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) now runs about 10x as often, which multiplies DB and IO load. The interval also no longer matches the 9-minute timeout in `clean()`, which was sized to fit inside a 10-minute cycle.
obligations: The full set of cleanup jobs must not run on a 1-minute cadence. Restoring the 10-minute interval (or something equivalent) satisfies this.
Keep the existing loop behavior: `cleanUpTmpFiles` runs once at startup, `srv.clean(ctx)` runs on each tick, and `ctx.Err()` is returned when the context is cancelled.
If a faster cadence is kept for some job (for example annotation cleanup), it must apply only to that job or be controlled by config. It must not speed up all jobs.
items.notes: The simplest valid fix is to revert to `time.Minute * 10`. Making the interval configurable with a 10-minute default is also fine. Ticks cannot overlap, because `clean` runs synchronously and Go tickers drop missed ticks. So the problem is load, not concurrency. The 9-minute timeout in `clean()` shows that 10 minutes was the intended interval. A fix that keeps 1 minute for every job does not resolve the finding.

items.defectStatement: In DualWriterMode3.Create, the background goroutine passes the result of d.Legacy.Create (errObjectSt) only to recordLegacyDuration as a boolean. The error itself is never logged. Before this PR, a failed legacy create was logged ("unable to create object in legacy storage"), so now legacy-store failures and drift happen silently.
obligations: When errObjectSt is non-nil, log it at error level, using the logger already in scope (`log`, or klog.FromContext(ctx), which carries the kind/method values) together with a descriptive message.
Keep the recordLegacyDuration call with errObjectSt != nil as its failure flag, and keep the same mode, kind, method and start-time arguments.
Keep the write asynchronous: do not block Create on the legacy write and do not return or propagate the legacy error to the caller. Create must still return created, err from Storage.
Do not log when errObjectSt is nil.
items.notes: The fix only has to cover the cited Create lines. The same omission exists in the Delete, Update and DeleteCollection goroutines, but fixing those is not required here. Any of these is acceptable: log.Error(...), klog.FromContext(ctx).Error(...), or log.WithValues("object", created).Error(...). Do not penalize the use of `log` captured from the outer scope. Unrelated issues the grader should not require fixes for: Create records recordLegacyDuration on a storage error, and DeleteCollection's goroutine calls recordStorageDuration.

items.defectStatement: In DualWriterMode3.Update, the background legacy write (line 139) passes the caller's original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update rather than the object already committed to unified storage (`res`). Legacy storage calls objInfo.UpdatedObject against its own old object, so a patch or transform gets applied again to legacy data that may be stale or different. The legacy store can then end up with a different object than unified storage, or the legacy update can fail, even though the unified update succeeded. The pre-PR code avoided this by wrapping the result in updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}.
obligations: The legacy Update call must receive an UpdatedObjectInfo whose UpdatedObject returns the object produced by the successful Storage.Update (`res`), not a recomputation from the original objInfo against the legacy old object (e.g. &updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}).
Preconditions must still come from the original objInfo (upstream), and the same name/createValidation/updateValidation/forceAllowCreate/options arguments must still be passed.

Keep the existing flow: the legacy update still runs asynchronously in the goroutine with its timeout context, legacy duration metrics are still recorded, and the function still returns res, async, err from unified storage.
items.notes: updateWrapper already exists in pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter.go (fields upstream and updated). Its UpdatedObject returns `updated`, and Preconditions delegates to upstream. Any equivalent wrapper that returns `res` is also acceptable. A fix that changes only line 139 is enough. Do not require changes to other bugs in this function (for example, recordLegacyDuration being used on the storage error path).

items.defectStatement: In DualWriterMode3.Delete (lines 99-105), every error from Storage.Delete makes the function return before Legacy.Delete runs, including NotFound. The old code treated NotFound from unified storage as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. Now an object that exists only in legacy storage is never deleted there and is left behind as an orphan.
obligations: When Storage.Delete returns an error that apierrors.IsNotFound recognizes, Legacy.Delete must still be called for the same name, deleteValidation and options (sync or in the existing background goroutine).

Errors from Storage.Delete that are not NotFound must still return right away without calling Legacy.Delete, and the storage-error metric/log must still be recorded. The existing test expects a generic storage error to be returned.
A successful Storage.Delete must keep its current behavior: record storage success, delete from legacy, and return res, async, err from storage.
items.notes: The fix needs the `apierrors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"` import back; the diff removed it. Mode2 Delete has a similar NotFound-tolerance pattern for reference. Several return values are valid when storage reports NotFound: returning the storage NotFound error (old behavior) or returning the legacy result. Either is fine as long as legacy deletion is attempted. A fix may also skip the error log or error metric when storage reports NotFound, but it doesn't have to. Other bugs nearby are outside this finding: the wrong metric name/arg on line 106 (passes `name` instead of the kind), `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` on line 97 using d.Log instead of log, and the goroutine using the request ctx, which may already be cancelled.

items.defectStatement: On line 106, the success path of DualWriterMode3.Delete passes `name` (the object name) as the third argument of recordStorageDuration. That argument fills the "kind" label of grafana_dual_writer_storage_duration_seconds. As a result the series is mislabeled, a new series is created for every deleted object name (unbounded cardinality), and it doesn't match the error path on line 103, which uses options.Kind.
obligations: The successful storage-delete metric must be recorded with the resource kind (options.Kind) as the kind label, not the object name.
Keep the rest of the call unchanged: isError=false, mode3Str, method "delete", and the startStorage timing on the storage histogram (not the legacy one).
Do not change the return values or the async legacy delete that runs after it.
items.notes: The fix is a one-token change: replace `name` with `options.Kind`. The same bug exists in dualwriter_mode1.go:155 (recordLegacyDuration with name), but it is outside the cited lines. The PR has other metric problems that are out of scope here: Create and Update record failures with recordLegacyDuration, and the DeleteCollection goroutine uses recordStorageDuration for the legacy call. Also out of scope: the Delete context is built from d.Log instead of log. A fix that only touches line 106 is fully correct.

items.defectStatement: `_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function`, which is Arroyo's `Commit` callback (`result_consumer.py` wraps it as `commit_offsets` and adds +1). That callback is not thread-safe: it changes StreamProcessor and consumer commit state, and Arroyo expects it to be called from the processor thread inside `submit`/`poll`/`join`. Calling it from a background thread races with `_run_once`/poll and with rebalancing, so offsets can be committed for partitions that were just revoked or after the strategy has been closed.
obligations: `commit_function` must no longer be called from the background thread while the processor thread may be running poll/submit. Either commits move to the strategy's main-thread callbacks (`poll()` and/or `submit()`, and possibly `join`/`close`), or every access is serialized by a lock that the main thread also holds around its strategy calls.

Offsets that are computed but not yet committed must not be marked committed until `commit_function` actually succeeds. `mark_committed` must still be called after a successful commit so that `last_committed` and pruning of `all_offsets` keep working.
Commits must stop once the strategy is closed or terminated, so no commit happens after shutdown or partition revocation.
Existing behavior must be kept: only contiguous completed offsets get committed, the `offsets_committed` metric is still emitted, and commit errors are logged rather than crashing the consumer.
items.notes: More than one fix is valid. (a) Remove the commit thread and commit from `poll()` on a ~1s throttle, which is the simplest and most idiomatic Arroyo approach. (b) Keep the thread but have it only compute offsets and hand them off, for example via a queue or an attribute, with `poll()` doing the actual commit. (c) Use a shared lock plus a closed flag. Option (c) is weak unless the lock also guards the main-thread calls into the consumer; a lock used only inside the thread does not fix the race. Note that the fix may have to touch lines outside the cited range: `__init__` thread start, `poll`, and `close`. A replacement limited to the cited lines alone (e.g. just wrapping the call in try/except) does not fix the defect. The `queue_pool`/offset tracker is shared across strategy instances because it is owned by the factory, so the closed check belongs on the strategy instance.

items.defectStatement: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but the `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared by every strategy from `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`. After a rebalance, arroyo closes the old strategy and builds a new one, and the new one gets a pool whose queues are shut down and whose workers have exited. Its `queue.put` then raises `ShutDown`, and `submit`'s except branch marks the offset as complete. The result is that messages get committed without ever being processed (silent data loss).
obligations: close() and terminate() must not leave the shared, factory-owned FixedQueuePool unusable for a strategy that `create_with_partitions` creates later. That means either not shutting down the shared pool there, or switching to a design where each strategy owns its own pool and the factory no longer shares one.
close() must still stop this strategy's commit thread (set shutdown_event and join it, as now), so the old strategy's commit thread doesn't keep calling a stale `commit` callback after close.
terminate() must still signal the commit thread to stop (shutdown_event set).

The pool must still be fully shut down when the consumer shuts down for good. Factory.shutdown() already does this, so a fix that only removes the pool shutdown from the strategy is acceptable as long as that path stays intact.
items.notes: The pool is created once in result_consumer.py:133 and is also shut down in factory.shutdown() (lines 183-185), so dropping `queue_pool.shutdown()` from the strategy's close/terminate is a valid minimal fix. Optional extras are fine but not required: waiting for the queues to drain (wait_until_empty) and doing one final commit inside close. Moving pool ownership into the strategy (a new pool per create_with_partitions) is also valid. The finding's claim of "multiple commit threads" is overstated: arroyo calls close before creating the next strategy, and close joins the commit thread. Only terminate skips the join, which could cause a brief overlap. Leftover OffsetTracker state for revoked partitions is a real but separate issue and is not required here.

items.defectStatement: FixedQueuePool creates each per-worker queue as an unbounded `queue.Queue()` (line 185), and `submit()` (lines 204-212) always enqueues without checking depth. When Kafka messages arrive faster than the worker threads finish them, the queues and the OffsetTracker sets keep growing with no limit, which can run the consumer out of memory. This also contradicts the "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" promise in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring.
obligations: Queue growth must be bounded: either the queues get a finite maxsize, or submit() checks depth or a limit before enqueueing. When a queue is full, the producer must be slowed down, either by a blocking put or by a signal such as raising arroyo's MessageRejected. Silently dropping the item is not acceptable.

Ordering and offset safety must be kept: each group_key still goes to the same queue in FIFO order. An offset must never be left in OffsetTracker as outstanding when its item was not actually enqueued (for example, if a put times out or raises Full). In that case, either add the offset only after a successful put, or roll it back.

Existing behavior must keep working: consistent hashing, worker startup, get_stats/qsize, wait_until_empty, and shutdown via queue.shutdown(). A blocking put must not deadlock shutdown forever; an unbounded block during shutdown is a concern.
items.notes: Several fixes are valid: a bounded Queue(maxsize=N) with a blocking put, which is simplest and works because the arroyo consumer thread is the only producer; a put with a timeout that then raises MessageRejected; or a qsize check before enqueueing that raises MessageRejected. The limit can be a constructor parameter with a default. Trap: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit wraps queue_pool.submit in `except Exception`, which logs the error and marks the offset complete. So if the pool raises MessageRejected or queue.Full, the message is dropped unless that caller re-raises it. The caller is outside the cited lines, so the grader should only flag this if the fix relies on raising and claims the message is not lost. Also, with add_offset placed before put, a failed put leaves an outstanding offset that stalls commits for that partition. The only production caller is result_consumer.py:133, which passes num_queues only, so any new parameter needs a default.

items.defectStatement: The finding is mostly overstated. In `submit()` (lines 293-325), a message whose payload is a FilteredPayload is sent to the decoder, and `decode_payload` raises an AssertionError for it. It is not true that every such message loses its offset. If the message is wrapped in a BrokerValue (the normal case), the `except` branch still calls add_offset/complete_offset, so the offset is tracked and committed. The offset is only dropped when the message value is a plain arroyo `Value` (not a BrokerValue), which is how arroyo's upstream filter steps emit filtered messages. Even when a filtered message does arrive, the code goes through a logged exception (`logger.exception`) instead of a clean skip.
obligations: Filtered messages (payload is a FilteredPayload) must not be passed to the decoder and must not produce an exception log. They need to be detected up front, before decoding, and skipped cleanly.

If a filtered message carries a broker partition/offset (a BrokerValue), that offset must still be marked complete (add_offset followed by complete_offset), so the commit loop can move past it and later offsets aren't held back.

Existing behavior for non-filtered KafkaPayload messages must not change: when the decoder returns None, the offset is added and completed immediately. Decoded results are grouped and submitted to the queue pool. If decoding fails, the error is logged and the offset is still completed.
items.notes: In this repo the strategy is the root step of the consumer (`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` in result_consumer.py), so it receives BrokerValue[KafkaPayload] straight from Kafka, and filtered payloads should not normally reach it. The finding's claim that filtered messages are skipped by the `except` branch is wrong for BrokerValue-wrapped messages, because that branch does record their offsets. It is only right for plain `Value` messages, which have no partition/offset of their own, only a `committable` mapping. A fix that adds an explicit `isinstance(message.payload, FilteredPayload)` check before calling the decoder, and completes the offset when the value is a BrokerValue, is acceptable. A fix that also handles a plain `Value` via `message.committable` is a valid extra but is not required. Do not penalize fixes that leave the outer try/except in place.

items.defectStatement: The final assertion in `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` (line 1922) checks that nothing was committed for the partition. In the real code, `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `complete_offset` in a `finally` block, so offset 100 counts as completed even though processing raised. Offsets 100 and 101 then form a contiguous completed run. On its next tick (it waits 1.0s each loop), `_commit_loop` passes 101 to `commit_offsets`, which adds 1 and commits {partition: 102}. The test passes only because its wait loop exits about 0.2s after the queues drain, before the commit thread wakes. So it is timing-dependent, it asserts the opposite of the real behavior, and it contradicts its own docstring ("errors don't block offset commits").
obligations: The test must wait until a commit has actually happened, polling up to a bounded timeout longer than the 1s commit interval (e.g. until `test_partition in committed_offsets`). It must not exit before the commit thread can run.
It must assert that `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`, meaning the failed message 100 does not block the commit and the next offset to read after 101 is committed.
It must keep the assertion that the processor was called exactly twice (`call_count == 2`), with the first call raising.
items.notes: The commit value is 102, not 101: `get_committable_offsets` returns the highest completed offset (101), and `result_consumer.commit_offsets` adds 1 to it. Any bounded wait is acceptable (polling on `committed_offsets`, a longer loop, or a threading.Event set in `track_commits`), as long as it reliably covers more than 1s. A fix that only lengthens the sleep but keeps asserting "no commit" is wrong. A fix that asserts a commit happened without checking the value 102 is weak. The fix is scoped to the cited lines in the test. Changing production code so that failed offsets are not completed would contradict the intended behavior stated in the docstring.

items.defectStatement: In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` (lines 86-96), the commit loop walks offsets one number at a time and stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka partitions can legitimately skip offsets (transaction control markers, compaction), and an offset that was never delivered is not outstanding work, yet it still stops the scan. The finding overstates the impact. Commits do not stop forever: once `mark_committed` drops offsets <= N, `min_offset` moves past the gap, so the next cycle resumes. But each 1-second commit cycle can only get past one gap. On topics with frequent gaps, commits fall further and further behind, and a gap holds back already-completed offsets for an extra cycle.
obligations: Offsets that were never delivered (missing from the tracked set) must not limit how far a commit can go. In a single call, the committable offset should be the highest completed offset that has no earlier tracked offset still outstanding, even if there are one or more numeric gaps between them.
An earlier tracked offset that is still outstanding must still block every offset after it (for example, 100 completed, 101 outstanding, 102 completed → commit 100 only).

The result must still be computed per partition, must only include partitions whose committable offset is greater than last_committed, and must stay correct after mark_committed prunes offsets (no committing at or below last_committed).
Offsets added and completed right away (filtered or failed decodes) must still count as completed, and the per-partition locking must be kept.
items.notes: A gap does not stall a partition forever: after mark_committed, start = max(last_committed+1, min(all_offsets)) jumps past it. So the real bug is that commits advance only one gap per cycle and lag on topics with many gaps. Several fixes are valid: iterate over sorted tracked offsets instead of range(), commit up to (smallest outstanding - 1) limited to tracked offsets, or keep an ordered deque per partition. An exact copy of the finding's deque design is not required. The existing test `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` submits 101 after 102/103 and expects the gap to block commits. That ordering cannot happen within one Kafka partition, and the current code already fails that expectation in a timing-dependent way. A correct fix may conflict with that test and should not be penalized for it. The separate question of whether to commit offset vs offset+1 is out of scope.

items.defectStatement: In OrderedQueueWorker.run (lines 144-149), the `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raises. The offset is then treated as done and gets committed, so a failed message is logged and skipped, never retried. This contradicts the strategy docstring's promise to "only commit offsets after successful processing". In practice the impact is limited: the production processor (`ResultProcessor.__call__` in `result_consumer.py`) already catches and logs every exception itself, so this `except` branch rarely runs.
obligations: On success, the offset must still be marked complete so commits keep moving forward (the existing tests test_offset_committing, which expects a commit at 104, and test_offset_gaps_block_commits must still pass).

When `result_processor` raises an ordinary Exception, the worker must not quietly treat the message as successfully processed. Either leave the offset outstanding (or otherwise stop the commit from moving past it), or retry or re-raise. Whatever the choice, the worker thread must stay alive, the exception must still be logged, and the queue-depth metric must still be emitted every iteration.
The `queue.ShutDown` handling and loop exit behaviour must be preserved.
items.notes: Treat the finding as partly overstated. The production ResultProcessor swallows its own exceptions, so 'permanent data loss for any processor that raises' only applies to processors that let exceptions escape. Completing on failure looks like a deliberate log-and-skip policy: `submit()` does the same when decoding fails, and the other consumer modes work the same way. The fix the finding suggests, leaving the offset outstanding, has a serious downside. Nothing retries the message, so that partition's commits stay blocked until a rebalance or restart, and lag grows without limit. A good fix should either accept this knowingly (blocking is preferred over loss) or add a retry. Both approaches are valid. Moving `complete_offset` into the try after the successful call, or guarding it with a success flag, both count. A fix that keeps `complete_offset` unconditional does not address the finding.

items.defectStatement: In SpanFlusher.join() (lines 337-347), once a timeout deadline has passed, the `break` leaves the loop. Every process not yet visited is then skipped: nothing waits on it and nothing calls terminate() on it. The old single-process code always called terminate() after waiting, so a hung flusher process is now left running after join() returns instead of being terminated.
obligations: After the deadline passes, every remaining process must still get the terminate step. No process in self.processes may be skipped because an earlier one used up the time.
Once the deadline has passed, no further time may be spent waiting (no more sleep/poll loops). Total waiting must stay bounded by the timeout.
When timeout is None, keep the current behavior: wait for each process to exit, then terminate it.
Keep the guard that only calls terminate() on process objects, never on threading.Thread instances, which have no terminate().
items.notes: Several fixes are valid: replace `break` with skipping the wait but still terminating; wait on all processes first and then terminate all in a second loop; or drop the early check, since the while-condition already stops waiting after the deadline. Any of these is fine as long as all processes reach terminate. Pre-existing issue, not required here: `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is probably False for SpawnProcess objects, because SpawnProcess subclasses BaseProcess, not context.Process. If so, terminate() may never actually run, before or after this change. A fix that changes the check to multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess, or uses hasattr(process, 'terminate'), is acceptable and arguably better. Do not mark a fix wrong for keeping the existing check, because the finding is about control flow. The unused `process_index`/`remaining_time` variables don't matter.

items.defectStatement: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` flag is on, `tableResultComponent` renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with hard-coded empty `data: []`, empty `meta.fields`/`units`, and `columns={[]}`. It never uses `result.data`, `result.meta` or `widget.queries[i]`, so every table widget shows nothing. Because an explicit `columns={[]}` overrides the component's fallback (which builds columns from `tableData.meta.fields`), the table also has zero columns.
obligations: The flagged branch must pass the current result's rows (`result.data`, per `i`, not a constant) as the visualization's `tableData.data`.
The flagged branch must pass real field types (and units, if available) taken from `result.meta` as `tableData.meta`, converted or defaulted as needed to fit the TabularData shape.
`columns` must not be an empty array. Either leave it out so the component derives columns from meta, or build it from `widget.queries[i]` fields and aliases, so the columns match the query.
The non-flagged `StyledSimpleTableChart` branch and its behavior must stay unchanged.
items.notes: Both fixes are valid: leaving out `columns` (the fallback reads `tableData.meta.fields`), or building `TabularColumn`s from the query fields and aliases. Any fix that keeps `columns={[]}` still renders no columns, even if it supplies the data. Loading state, custom renderers and units do not have to match the old table exactly. This looks like a placeholder for a feature-flagged rollout, but the grader should still require real data to be wired in.

items.defectStatement: The react-query key for attribute keys is ['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions], and queryOptions contains only itemType, attributeType, project, substringMatch and the datetime params. It has no organization identifier, yet the queryFn calls `/organizations/${organization.slug}/trace-items/attributes/`. Two orgs with the same filters (for example selection.projects = [] meaning all projects, with the same period and type) therefore share a cache entry, so one org can be shown the other org's cached TagCollection. The old useApiQuery key avoided this because it included the org-scoped path.
obligations: The queryKey must include something org-specific (such as organization.slug, organization.id or the org-scoped URL path), so different orgs with otherwise identical options get separate cache entries.
The key must still include queryOptions (or the same fields: traceItemType, type, projectIds, datetime), so changing filters still triggers a new fetch.
